description: Refined, PII-free pet health FAQ knowledge base derived from customer support correspondence. Rewritten as generalized Q&A pairs suitable for chatbot ingestion.

records.question: My dog has itchy skin and we've tried multiple elimination diets through skin specialists without success. What else can we try?
records.answer: Without knowing the cause of the itching, start at the beginning with a completely hypoallergenic diet that removes the four major causes of itching, irritation and inflammation. Remove all treats and other foods during the trial. After three to four weeks, one of three things should happen: complete improvement suggests a food allergy; partial improvement suggests a combination of food and contact or environmental allergies; and no improvement suggests a contact or environmental allergy rather than food. The result gives us a direction so we can recommend treatments, products and solutions for your dog's specific issues.

records.question: My dog is itchy around the eyes, face, muzzle and ears. Could this be food related?
records.answer: Absolutely, it could be a food allergen. However, itching around the eyes, face, muzzle and ears can also be caused by contact or environmental allergens. Many dogs roll in grass or other things that may set them off. A hypoallergenic diet trial can help assess whether the cause is food, contact or environmental.

records.question: My dog's itching gets worse in spring and summer but clears up over winter. What does this mean?
records.answer: This suggests a contact or environmental allergen. Grass grows quickly in spring and summer and can cause skin issues, while seasonal pollen can cause symptoms such as itchy or goopy eyes. The fact that the itching clears over winter is quite indicative of a seasonal contact allergy. Products that support the immune system and skin microbiome can help manage it.

records.question: My dog has a yeasty smell and their skin gets worse in summer. What could be causing this?
records.answer: Yeast issues can have several causes. Dogs with food or contact allergens become itchy and lick sensitive areas such as their armpits or paws. Saliva remains in those warm areas and can develop into a yeast infection. Scratching can then transfer it between the feet and ears. Food does not create yeast issues, but certain foods can be used to help starve the yeast, alongside support for the immune system and gut health.

records.question: My dog is licking their paws and rolling around a lot. What are the common causes?
records.answer: First assess whether the dog is itchy over the whole body or mainly on the underbelly, undercarriage and paws. This helps distinguish a possible food and contact allergy from a contact allergy alone. The itching can then be relieved with appropriate diet changes or supplements that support dogs with contact and seasonal allergies.

records.question: Even organic beef seems to cause my dog's allergies. Is that normal?
records.answer: Yes. Feeding organic beef or chicken does not prevent a food-allergy reaction because dogs are allergic to the protein in the meat. Even when the animal was raised organically, a dog that reacts to that meat protein can still have an adverse reaction.

records.question: My terrier has chronic itching. Are certain breeds more prone to allergies?
records.answer: Absolutely. Terriers are particularly prone to food and contact allergies, and colouration can be a factor, especially with dilute colours such as blue. Other breeds, including German Shepherds and Shar-Peis, can also have sensitive skin, but terriers are certainly among the breeds more prone to these issues.

records.question: My dog has chronic skin issues (belly, groin, armpit, neck) and is now getting recurring ear infections. Could switching food help?
records.answer: This pattern sounds like contact allergens, although food allergens may also be involved. A food allergen would usually cause itching across more of the body, while the belly, feet, armpits and groin have thinner hair and more contact with grass and sap. Dogs then lick the itchy areas, and the warm saliva between their feet can lead to a yeast infection, sometimes with an orange or rusty tint and an unusual smell. Scratching can transfer the yeast between the feet and ears. Food does not cause yeast, but selected foods can help starve it, while immune support and better-quality food can help reduce discomfort.
records.safety_note: Recurring ear infections and chronic skin issues that don't improve with diet changes should be assessed by a vet.

records.question: Is it okay to keep my dog on a topical itch spray alongside a prescribed allergy medication?
records.answer: For the most part, yes, although we would double-check the particular medication and topical product. We can also reassess the cause of the allergy and look at ways to reduce the dog's need for medication or potentially come off it entirely, while keeping the dog comfortable.
records.safety_note: Always check with your vet before combining any new topical or supplement with prescribed medication.

records.question: How do I bathe my itchy dog without making the itching worse?
records.answer: Some vet-prescribed products, such as Malaseb, soothe the skin and coat effectively, but they can also strip microbes from the skin. When the skin flora rebuilds, the unwanted microbes may return first. For regular bathing, choose something gentle and natural that does not strip the skin. The WashBar range is a gentle option with antibacterial, antimicrobial and antifungal properties.

records.question: My dog got sick after eating a smoked treat. Could the smoking process be the cause?
records.answer: It could be the smoking process, but that is unlikely. A more likely cause is that the dog is not used to the treat's flavour, has a sensitive stomach, or was introduced to the treat or protein too quickly. Nausea, vomiting and eating grass can be signs of this kind of stomach upset.

records.question: What's a good hypoallergenic protein option if I need to buy in bulk for multiple dogs?
records.answer: If you know which protein causes the itching, choose an alternative that is free from that protein, such as a food without beef, chicken or wheat. If the allergen is unknown, start with stage one of a hypoallergenic diet trial. For value, Natura Diet Itch Buster and Natura Diet Grain Be Gone are fully hypoallergenic options made in New Zealand from wild-caught New Zealand fish. Once the cause of the itching is understood, we may be able to suggest cheaper alternatives.

records.question: My dog is a fussy eater and isn't taking to a new hypoallergenic food. What should I try?
records.answer: There are many reasons for fussy eating, and some veterinary hypoallergenic foods are not especially rich in flavour or available in alternative flavours. We have several options for different dogs, including Natura Diet Itch Buster, Natura Diet Grain Be Gone and multiple hypoallergenic Addiction flavours. Addiction's small biscuit sizes can suit small, fussy dogs, while Grain Be Gone and Itch Buster offer good value for medium and large breeds.

records.question: My dog has IBD and is limited to single-protein exotic meats. What should I know about ingredient changes?
records.answer: For dogs with food sensitivities and gut-health issues, start by supporting the gut microbiome with good probiotics and prebiotics, then choose gentle meats. Natura Diet Itch Buster is our leading option: it is hypoallergenic and has been independently tested to universal standards for dogs with impaired gut health, gastrointestinal issues, impaired liver function, and dogs with or prone to pancreatitis. This makes it a useful multifaceted option for dogs with IBD.
records.safety_note: For dogs with a vet-diagnosed condition like IBD, confirm any recipe or ingredient change with your vet before feeding.

records.question: My dog is bored of eating the same food. What can I do to add variety without upsetting their stomach?
records.answer: If your dog is on a hypoallergenic diet, anything on our website marked with a pink-purple circle is safe for them. Dogs on sensitive or hypoallergenic diets do not have to miss out. We have taken the guesswork out of choosing treats, raw food, tinned food, wet food and food toppers that are suitable for dogs with itching, skin issues, food allergies or sensitive stomachs. Follow the colour coding on the website or the barcodes in store to give your dog safe variety.

records.question: Why might my dog get bored of a food after being on it for a while?
records.answer: Like humans, dogs have different tastes. Smaller dogs can become fussy because we often treat them more like little people, giving them special tidbits, home-cooked food and the best of everything. They learn that if they hold out, their owner may offer something better. Most dogs also enjoy variety, so adding a wet food or topper, or alternating between appropriate options, can keep meals exciting and maintain their interest.

records.question: My dog has multiple food allergies. Are treats safe to give as well?
records.answer: Absolutely. We have taken out the guesswork: anything on our website with a pink-purple circle, or a pink-purple barcode in store, indicates a hypoallergenic option. These products exclude the four main causes: wheat, chicken, beef, and processing additives such as colourings, flavourings and preservatives.

records.question: How do I figure out which protein my dog is allergic to?
records.answer: The standard approach is an elimination diet: start with a novel protein your dog hasn't eaten before (such as kangaroo or lamb), feed it exclusively for several weeks, and watch for improvement. If symptoms improve, you can then reintroduce previous proteins one at a time to identify the trigger. This narrows things down from a clean baseline rather than guessing.

records.question: My dog has environmental sensitivities as well as food ones. What can help?
records.answer: First, put the dog on a correctly balanced hypoallergenic diet. Then use products that support environmental sensitivities, such as BioPet grasses and WashBar Itch Soothe topical spray, to soothe itchy areas and reduce inflammation. A microbiome prebiotic can also help get gut health back on track. Better gut health supports the immune system, helping the dog cope with contact or grass allergies. You cannot eliminate a grass or contact allergy, but these options can reduce the problem and discomfort.

records.question: My dog has ongoing diarrhoea even after switching food. What should I check?
records.answer: Diarrhoea is often associated with a poor gut microbiome. Anaesthetic, steroids, prednisone, other medication and stress can all affect the stomach lining and gut health. Start with a prebiotic or probiotic to help restore gut health, and use a hypoallergenic food to reduce inflammation. New foods can then be reintroduced slowly while assessing possible causes. Dogs should not have constant vomiting or diarrhoea; unless a condition such as IBD has been diagnosed, we can resolve 99% of these issues permanently.
records.safety_note: Persistent diarrhoea, especially if it continues for more than a few days or is accompanied by other symptoms, should be assessed by a vet.

records.question: Can a change in protein help firm up my dog's stool?
records.answer: Absolutely. Richer proteins can sometimes produce looser stools, so changing the protein may help. Increasing bone content is another natural way to firm the stool. For anal-gland issues, OmegaFlex pumpkin powder can help firm loose stools or soften stools when the dog is constipated. This can support natural anal-gland emptying and reduce related issues.

records.question: My large-breed puppy is 9 months old. Should I switch them to adult food now or wait?
records.answer: In general, large-breed puppies should stay on puppy food until at least 12 months old. By nine months they are close to their mature height, but this is when they begin adding mass, building bulk and increasing bone density, so extra calcium and protein remain important. You could move to an adult food if it is very high in protein and fat and you provide additional bone, but it is best to have a chat about the individual puppy first.

records.question: My puppy isn't very food motivated and is slow to adjust to a new food. Is that normal?
records.answer: Depending on the puppy's age and breed, this can be completely normal. Changing a young puppy's food too quickly can cause stomach upset, so make the transition slowly. Some puppies simply are not highly food-motivated. As long as the puppy is healthy and growing consistently along its expected growth trend, there should not be a problem.

records.question: I noticed my bag of food looks or smells slightly different from the last one. Is that a problem?
records.answer: Because we use natural products and natural food preservatives, there can be slight variations in the food's colour and smell. Seasonal ingredients, including fish, can also create differences in colour. Small variations in tone and appearance are normal, and the food should still be fine.
records.safety_note: If you notice visible mould, an off smell, or your pet has an adverse reaction after eating a specific bag, stop feeding it and contact the manufacturer with the batch number.

records.question: Why did the ingredient list on a product change?
records.answer: Manufacturers do occasionally reformulate a recipe, which can mean small changes to ingredients or moisture content even if the overall product name stays the same. If your pet has specific dietary restrictions, it's worth comparing the old and new ingredient list side by side whenever you're unsure, rather than assuming the recipe is unchanged.

records.question: Is it cheaper to buy dog food in bulk?
records.answer: If you run a kennel, breeding business, doggy day care or similar operation and want to buy bulk stock, we can help. We also offer great pricing for individuals who want to buy dog food in bulk for their own pets.

records.question: My dog is overweight for their breed. What kind of food change can help?
records.answer: Weight gain is generally a matter of calories in versus calories out. Some breeds have slower metabolisms, and some dogs gain weight after desexing, but the most common cause is overfeeding through snacks and tidbits during the day. Usually, reducing the total quantity is the first step. Larger biscuits can slow eating and make the meal more satisfying than small biscuits that are gulped down. We also have low-fat foods and treats, so the dog does not need to go on a strict diet; they just need the right proteins and portions.

records.question: How many treats or treat-sticks can I give without overdoing calories?
records.answer: Our treats are natural and clean, so they generally act as protein substitutes. If you feed more treats, reduce the amount of regular food because the treats are also nutritionally beneficial. Too many treats can reduce the balance of the overall diet, so a good-quality raw or kibble food should remain the priority, with treats used as a top-up and for enjoyment.

records.question: What's the difference between a grain-free and a wheat-free hypoallergenic food?
records.answer: Grain-free became a major marketing trend about ten years ago, but most dogs are not allergic to grains. In 99.9% of dogs with food issues or allergies, wheat is the problem, so wheat-free is usually the important requirement. Grain-free food is slightly cleaner and may be needed by the small percentage of dogs that react to other grains. Its main benefit is for dogs with yeast issues: food does not cause yeast, but grains break down into sugars that can feed it. Grain-free food produces less sugar and can help starve the yeast. In short, choose grain-free for yeasty issues and wheat-free for typical allergy issues.
